text: Chapter 24, S3-like object storage. Let's see how it works in a few minutes.

Object storage keeps data in buckets. A bucket is a logical container with a globally unique name. An object is data plus metadata, found by its key. The slashes in a key are just a prefix convention, not real directories. Objects are written whole and replaced whole. No in-place edits.

The core idea of this chapter: separate metadata from data. Metadata is the small stuff, bucket name, object name, object ID. The actual bytes live in the data store, fetched by object ID. It's like UNIX: look up the inode first, then read the blocks. Once split, each side can scale on its own.

On upload, the request goes through a load balancer to a stateless API service. The API asks IAM to check identity and write permission, hands the bytes to the data store, and gets back an object ID. Last, it records the bucket, name, and that ID in the metadata store. A download reverses it: look up the ID in metadata, then fetch the bytes.

Inside the data store, a routing service asks the placement service which node should take the write. Small objects aren't stored one file each. They're appended into a big file of a few gigabytes. A local index records the object ID, file name, start offset, and size. To read, look up the index and jump straight to the bytes.

Now durability. Erasure coding splits an object into eight data chunks, then computes four parity chunks. That's twelve chunks, each placed on a different disk in a different failure domain. This is called eight plus four.

Disks fail. Even if four chunks are lost at once, any eight survivors, data or parity, can rebuild the original object. But lose one more, and only seven remain. Recovery is impossible. So the twelve chunks must be spread across racks and data centers, so that no single failure takes out five.

Compare that with three-way replication. Three copies cost triple the space, two hundred percent extra. Eight plus four costs one and a half times, just fifty percent extra. The book assumes a yearly disk failure rate of zero point eight one percent. Replication gives about six nines, while the cited model puts erasure coding at eleven nines. The cost is more complex encoding, and reads that span many nodes. Latency-sensitive systems lean toward replication. Cost-sensitive, large-scale storage leans toward erasure coding.

Large files use multipart upload. First, initiate, and get an upload ID. Then split the file into parts and upload each independently. Each success returns an ETag. If one part fails, retry only that part. When all are done, submit the upload ID with part numbers and ETags, and only then does the server assemble the object. Leftover temporary parts go to garbage collection.

Object versioning. Uploading to the same key doesn't overwrite. It adds a new version, with a new object ID and a time-ordered version number. Reads return the latest by default. A delete doesn't erase bytes. It inserts a delete marker, so a default read returns four oh four. Older versions remain, and you can still read them by version number.

To sum up. Separate metadata from data: names look up metadata, IDs look up data nodes. Erasure coding buys high durability for one and a half times the space, if chunks span failure domains. Multipart upload and versioning make large files and accidental deletes easy to handle.
